title: The Builsa: The People Who Stopped the Raiders

pages.text: Each December, in the town of Sandema in the Upper East Region, men march into the durbar ground dressed for war. They wear smocks covered with charms and helmets fitted with the horns of bulls and antelopes. They carry bows, quivers of arrows, axes, and spears. To the beat of drums and the scream of whistles, they stamp, crouch, and charge at an enemy nobody can see. This is the Feok festival of the Builsa people. The enemy they are fighting again is one their great-grandfathers faced in real life: a slave raider named Babatu.

pages.text: The Builsa lived in farming villages spread across the savanna. They grew millet and guinea corn, kept cattle, and built flat-roofed houses of mud, joined into large compounds. For most of their history they had no king over all of them. Each village looked after its own affairs under its elders and its earth priest. This suited a peaceful life. It was a weakness when danger came, because a village standing alone could be attacked and destroyed before its neighbours even heard the news. There was no army to send and no one to call for help.

pages.text: Danger came in the second half of the 1800s. Bands of horsemen known as the Zabarima rode in from the lands that are now Niger. First they came as traders and hired soldiers. Then they turned to raiding. Under their leader Babatu, they attacked village after village across the north, among the Sissala, the Kasena, and the Builsa. They burned houses and seized grain and cattle. Worst of all, they carried off men, women, and children to be sold as slaves in distant markets. Whole districts were emptied as people fled.

They burned houses and seized grain and cattle.

Whole districts were emptied as people fled.
pages.alt: Horsemen with guns riding hard towards a village as smoke rises from its granaries.

pages.text: People defended themselves in different ways. At Gwollu, the Sissala built two rings of high mud wall around their town and its farms. Parts of that wall can still be seen. Others hid in caves or among rocks. The Builsa chose to unite. Messages went from village to village. Fighters gathered at Sandema, armed with bows and poisoned arrows, and prepared for the raiders. Tradition says that the women played their part by carrying water, food, and arrows to the men. When Babatu’s horsemen came, in about 1896, the Builsa were ready.

pages.alt: The remains of a high mud wall curving round a village, with a baobab tree beside it.

pages.text: The battle went against the raiders. Horses are of little use among rocks, thick bush, and walls, and guns of that time were slow to reload. The Builsa archers shot from cover and drove the horsemen back with heavy losses. Babatu retreated. He never returned to Builsa country. Soon afterwards, British and French forces, who were then taking control of the region, broke what was left of his army. The raids ended. For the Builsa, the lesson was clear, and the chief of Sandema came to be recognised as the leader of all the Builsa.

pages.text: Feok means plenty of food. The festival gives thanks for the harvest, and it remembers the victory at the same time. That is fitting. A people who are free to stay on their land can plant and harvest in peace. Slave raiding in the north is part of the same terrible history as the slave trade on the coast, and both deserve to be remembered. The Builsa story adds something hopeful to that history. Ordinary farmers, without a king or an army, protected their families by standing together. No village could have done it alone.

activities.question: Why were the Builsa villages easy to attack at first?
options: Each village stood alone, with no ruler over all of them

activities.question: What made the Zabarima raids so terrible?
options: They carried people off to be sold as slaves
They bought all the cattle at high prices
They built walls round the villages

activities.question: Why did the horsemen lose at Sandema?
options: Archers shot from cover, where horses and slow guns were of little use

activities.question: Apply it: Thieves keep stealing from farms in a community, one farm at a time. Which lesson from the Builsa is most useful?
options: Each farmer should guard only his own farm
The farmers should organise together and warn one another

activities.prompt: Put these events in order, from earliest to latest.
items: The Builsa live in separate farming villages
Zabarima horsemen arrive as traders and hired soldiers
Babatu’s raiders attack villages across the north
The Builsa unite and defeat the raiders at Sandema
The chief of Sandema is recognised as leader of all the Builsa
